en: A hero who never retreats,
And the very embodiment
Of our mortal enemy.
He scoured the land in a dreadful state
And has now ridden away.
He has the thoroughbred Kerik;
If you would fight, that is your foe,
And he alone has the strength of a thousand men.
Would he refrain from bringing grief?
That snarling infidel’s
Battle cry is ‘Kakanchi!’
Would such an enemy stand idle?
That terrifying villain’s
Battle cry is ‘Bakburchun!’
He speaks a strange, rambling tongue;
I understood nothing of it.
My hero Seytek, hear me!
He seized the livestock grazing in the mountains,
And took the lives of multitudes;
He killed the men who guarded the horses,
And took possession of the broad land,
Killing many splendid warriors.
Here I have finally arrived!”
Erebai gasped these words.
“So this is your report, Erebai:
The forces of Beijing have come!”
The power that threw the nation into turmoil—
For from ancient times Great Beijing
Had begun disputes and stirred up strife,
A custom inherited from its forefathers.
The enemy who would never come when sought
Had now come of his own accord to attack;
Without tormenting themselves, they had found him.
Your wish has been fulfilled,
Your enemy has fallen into your hands,
My tiger Seytek, now ride forth,
Good fortune has attended your campaign.
Your vanished enemy has returned,
This alone was your desire,
What you watched for has been granted”—
So saying, Akjoltoy
Mounted the swift steed Külansur,
Knotting up its flowing tail,
Revealing himself as a true hero,
Hearing news of the infidel,
He laughed aloud in delight,
And donned his battle gear.
That noble hero, wolf of war,
Rejoiced at the thought of death,
Through a broad ravine where no hawk flew,
Through a broad ravine where no bird flew,
The warriors raised a ringing cry
From their brass spears,
Speaking these words in earnest.
Our tiger, forefather Jолтой,
Our elder took to the road,
Fiercely raging,
Wearing a helmet of blue steel,
Its crown crested with tassels,
Its cheek guards fitted tight,
Contrived in every way
Never to fall from his head,
Its fastenings crossed,
And knotted beneath his throat.
Upon your impetuous elder Joltoy
Was armor no bullet could pierce.
He made Külansur prance,
And rode along broad Talas,
His stirrups clattering,
While the hard black earth beneath him
Thundered without pause,
Like the surging current of a river.
Kutubiy’s Akjoltoy
Was Seytek’s inheritance,
Himself a keen-eyed falcon;
If calamity befell his noble head,
He would stand beneath the banner
Of the honored Kyrgyz people.
Akjoltoy rode shouting,
A wondrous figure to behold,
Alone worth an army of thousands.
As he departed broad Talas,
His bearing and grandeur
Seemed unlike anyone among the people,
His stature tall as a minaret;
He could not rest without meeting the foe.
Since this Akjoltoy arose,
The enemy had not yet felt his wrath,
Nor had anyone traversed and subdued
Talas with all its multitude.
No foe had yet advanced against it,
No mortal had yet called it disaster.
The enemy who coveted Talas,
A grim and woeful host,
Had not yet cast its watery lasso.
Since Akjoltoy and Seytek arose,
They had not yet entered battle together.
To crush the raiders from the Kalmyks
And break their marching ranks,
Joltoy set out, dark with wrath.
Traveling by night, not by day,
He left the Kyrgyz people behind;
His strength and valor,
When observed, were beyond compare.
He roared in wounded pride,
Raising the battle cry without fail,
Raging and surging,
While the beast flew like a whirlwind,
And he spoke to Külansur:
“Since I became Akjoltoy,
Since Akjoltoy first mounted a horse,
I have not ridden on a distant campaign,
Nor charged the enemy with a shout.
They fed you rice as grain,
Saying, ‘Let him ride when he longs for holy war,’
And you came to me from the spirit realm.
You have never spread your flanks in a ravine,
Nor traveled a hard and distant road,
Nor learned how far it may be.
Ah, noble beast Külansur,
You are my comrade, sharing death;
You will lower your head to the earth
And boldly lengthen your stride.
A whip is the rider’s one support,
But when disaster befalls a precious life,
A hero’s purpose is something else.
Now I descend into the open steppe;
May my livestock be sacrificed for my life.
They have raided the borders of my people,
So I have mounted you in mastery, Külansur,
Saying, ‘My true beast is my comrade’;
I have mounted you in ardor, Külansur.”
So saying, Akjoltoy
Began to shout;
Rage seized his wretched soul,
And for pride and honor
He staked his life upon a hair.
Chonbilgich, who had come from afar,
Relentlessly began his oppression.
To behold Chonbilgich,
To fight without tiring,
To contend with him in open combat—
It was already too late to hesitate.
Against that warrior of perfect strength,
That infidel raider Bilgich,
Who stole horses and ruined nations,
He would unleash his deadly wrath;
If he found a way, he would
Win the horses back,
But if Akjoltoy could not,
He would take the road of no return,
Never again to live in health,
But simply surrender his life;
Though they were thousands, he would attack
And test his weight against them.
He traveled along the hills,
His anger hot enough to burn stone,
His surging force enough to topple mountains,
Straining onward without pause.
Alone from all his host, Akjoltoy
Quarreled with Külansur.
Here was the place for the whip,
The black-edged buldursun.
Its grip was smooth as glass,
Its wrist loop richly tasseled;
The hide of a sturdy three-year-old bull
Was stretched along its core.
The hide of a yellow-hoofed young buck
Was tightly braided around it.
A gray wolf’s sinew was set in its tip,
The braider had tightened and finished it,
Designing it for a foe in combat.
The black-edged buldursun,
When it struck, deafened the ears.
He seized it and swung,
Then drew up Külansur, who had never felt a whip,
And lashed him behind the thigh.
At that moment, when the sharp whip
Struck the racehorse,
Its flesh parted like a sheep’s,
Its back straightened like a lamb’s,
And it opened its mouth with a roar;
Behind it, a great cloud of dust
Spread out like a house along the road.
It flew forward roaring,
While the black earth rolled over
And shimmered behind it.
They drew near to Bilgich,
Whose multitude made the earth sag.
When he saw Akjoltoy’s tumult,
Bilgich roared, pouring out his wrath,
As though a nightmare had crushed his wife;
With a fearsome display, Bilgich
Summoned his champions:
“Drive the captured horses
By night and rest them by day;
Scout the land without losing hope.
Slaughter a colt for your provisions,
Make camp and post sentries.
Let us fortify our lives,
And after seizing all their horses,
Let us earn the praise
Of the renowned Khan Kite.
When summer comes, let us ask
For the rank of governor.
Let every heart be satisfied,
And every deed be brought to light;
Let it be written in the record
Of the great ones of your nation:
‘We avenged our fathers
And slaughtered the Buruts.’
There is no infidel like Akjoltoy,
And no wisdom in an empty breast.
Do not spoil the horses’ condition;
Keep driving them onward.
In six or seven days
There will be time to tether sheep—
Mark well these words of mine.
As for your ruler Bilgich,
When eight full days have passed,
Then you will know his fate.”
He said this to his warriors,
Telling grim horrors to those who understood,
Telling it to the bloodthirsty
Among his living men,
Telling it to those bloodstained warriors
Who crushed all they confronted.
To the heroes who did not flinch
When the fierce gun cracked,
To the champions who never fled from birth
When the black musket thundered,
He spread his hands and strode about,
Entrusting every detail
Of the turmoil that would follow.
He taunted some,
Confirmed the words of others,
And they pledged themselves.
For the Kakanchin realm was mighty,
And thus they stood together,
Speaking as though they guarded the world,
Binding the whole fleeting world
Firmly within their words.
Before Bilgich had closed his mouth,
Before he finished ordering the champions
To drive the horses onward,
Before he rebuked the foolish,
Encouraged the wise,
And finished speaking,
A shout arose from the qibla side.
When they heeded that cry,
They saw a lone man appear,
One who dwelt in the Ala-Too,
Whom no man could defeat in combat,
Who would not surrender his comrade’s life.
“God forbid we see his face!”
He raised the cry of “Kyrgyz!”
